subsequentEdits.reason: Owner's decision on what recovery needs: with the default settings only the container and the password; a non-default PIM or memory level must be remembered and may be kept secret; the suite identifier and the settings are no longer to be kept next to the container or apart from it. Owner's decision before the release: the specification no longer says that it has not been proposed as a BIP, and implementation version 0.4.0 is no longer called unreleased. Owner's wording in Motivation: the owner remembers a strong password, for example four or five dice words, instead of a 'randomly generated' one. Owner's decision to merge three overlapping Motivation points into two, with the offline-guessing warning given once and the decoy left to its own point. Owner's decision to add plausible deniability through decoy passwords: a Deniability section in the supplement with two experiments, lemmas and proofs, the matching Motivation point, related-work and security-summary sentences, and reference [46]. Owner's decision before the release: version 0.3.1 is no longer called unreleased, and the changelog gives its date. Security Considerations separate the deniability analysis from the conjectures and state its conditions and limits. Owner's decision before the release: the specification version becomes 0.4.0 instead of 0.3.1, because suite 3 changes the protocol. The suite 2 appendix points to the archive and to the research idea in the supplement. The state-derived salts are related to NIST SP 800-132, reference [48], and to RFC 9106, without claiming conformance. Owner's decision after the threat-model review: intermediate values, including Argon2id working memory, must not be written to persistent storage, error reports or resume files; a password is used for one container only; recomputation by an independent implementation checks a result but not leaks; long-term storage allows for guesses becoming cheaper. After a further review: the deniability summary separates the exact equality of the disclosed data from what the general bound adds, salt uniqueness is stated for containers of independently generated sources, and the verifier is said to screen most accidental corruption rather than damage in general. Owner's decision after the deniability review: the summary names what the analysis does not cover, asks for exact copies of one verified container and for no contradicting record of the phrase, and adds reference [49]. Owner's decision after a review of likely questions: why only the English wordlist, why NFKD, why Argon2id's secret and associated data are empty, when the container's own wallet can serve as a decoy instead of 'a decoy holding a small amount', and references [50] and [51]. Owner's decision after the same review: letter case and the characters between words of a password are significant after NFKD, with examples of variants for recovery assistance and the reason why words are read forgivingly, and the rehearsal reads the container from the finished backup. The copying-error estimate is stated for a random one-word substitution, and the comparison with a known address is named as what reveals a wrong 24-word container. Editorial review: one password per encrypted phrase with exact copies of a container, the check of the finished backup as its own requirement, the deniability summary in three paragraphs, the composition formulas left to the supplement, and clearer wording for the implementation version and the vector requirements. The English-only rationale cites BIP39's own recommendation against other wordlists, in its Wordlists section. After the release of v0.4.0: the banner names the release and its Zenodo DOI, 10.5281/zenodo.23074882, and the badge shows that DOI. The Test Vectors section names vectors/archive/suite-2/ for the archived suite 2 vectors. After the check of every cited source against its original: the Cryptosteel capsule has a fixed capacity for character tiles rather than a fixed number of words; the password advice says that EFF suggests six words and that four or five follow from the cost of an MHFE guess; the alternatives to a balanced Feistel network are described through sufficient published bounds rather than proven minimums; plausible deniability is modeled on deniable encryption and is narrower, since the decoy phrase is whatever the decoy password recovers; reference [36] names the full version with appendices, ePrint 2010/301, revision of November 29, 2018. Renumbered the common bibliography by first citation in README.md followed by DESIGN-NOTES.md, preserving every citation-to-source association and all bibliographic content. Owner's decision to add the length-preserving suite 4, MHFE-BIP39-LP-EXPERIMENTAL-4, after release 0.4.0 and outside it: a 12- to 21-word source becomes a container of the same word count with ENT/2-bit Feistel halves, the suite 3 Argon2id parameters, ENT in the salt and mask messages and no verifier; suite 3 stays the default and unchanged; recovery selects the suite by word count only within a workflow that supports both; the abstract, the decoy paragraph, Rationale, Security Considerations and Test Vectors state which suite they concern, and suite 4 vectors will follow with its implementation. After review of suite 4: the RFC 9106 salt-length remark is context rather than justification; a plain table explains which containers a chosen length or suite admits to recovery; Motivation names both container forms; the notation and the main procedure are scoped to suite 3; suite 4 vectors cover the settings and fast refusal cases. The suite 4 corpus is imported into vectors/suite4/; the banner and Test Vectors point to it. The deniability analysis is extended to suite 4; only the conjectures on attack cost are not asserted for it. Recorded the pending prior-art and citation corrections and bounded address-reference wording, then corrected the research proposals: container-digest notation, repair estimates and enumeration limits, independently trusted seals, settings-only checks, entropy-conditioning and nested-layer costs. Qualified mixed-KDF procedure costs; documented private password check words, bounded selection, recovery dependencies, independent emergency routes and intermediate state widths. Moved Research directions after implementation, vectors and limitations. These are subsequent document edits, not an extension of the original audit conclusions. 2026-10-05: User-authorized application requirements now require confirmation of the recovered source before re-encryption, an independent reference for a replacement with no source verifier, universal confirmation that affected derived wallets are preserved, and rehearsal of the replacement before treating it as checked or discarding an earlier backup. Old containers are not revoked. Targeted corrections on 2026-10-06 consolidate the two reviewers' wording findings; suite algorithms, fenced formulas, vectors and bibliography are unchanged. Targeted optional-profile wording corrections on 2026-10-06 clarify repair decoding limits and candidate counts, password check-word disclosure, and profile status; algorithms and public vectors are unchanged. Clarified MHFE-REPAIR-1 wording: even parity counts are a profile choice, a BIP39 checksum does not guarantee detection of a wrong repair, and a verified exact copy yields the same card. Code, parameters and vectors are unchanged. Consolidated all three optional-profile public vector sets and repair examples under Test Vectors, with reciprocal section links and contents entries; vector values and profile definitions are unchanged. Moved the three optional-profile tables and examples unchanged to vectors/profiles/README.md; the specification retains concise coverage descriptions and links, and the vector index links the new file. Clarified that the container has no explicit suite/version label while word count, source checks and wallet references can help assess recovery within their stated scope; suite definitions and mandatory rules are unchanged. Owner-authorized clarification of suite identification and all five document-review remarks: six-position password repair and general validation, conditional multi-container reuse estimates, historical suite 3 implementation scope and current vector links, and limitations of both suites and the optional profiles. Prepared specification version 0.5.0 as unreleased, with consistent preamble, banner, changelog and citation metadata; the v0.4.0 DOI and release date remain archival. Algorithms and vector values are unchanged. Added a specification version 0.5.0 badge next to the license badges, linking the changelog. Suite algorithms and public vector values are unchanged.

subsequentEdits.reason: Owner's decision on what recovery needs: with the default settings only the container and the password; a non-default PIM or memory level must be remembered and may be kept secret; the suite identifier and the settings are no longer to be kept next to the container or apart from it. Owner's decision to add plausible deniability through decoy passwords: a Deniability section in the supplement with two experiments, lemmas and proofs, the matching Motivation point, related-work and security-summary sentences, and reference [46]. States that BLAKE2b and SHA-256 stay shared in the games of the deniability proof. Owner's decision before the release: the specification version becomes 0.4.0 instead of 0.3.1, because suite 3 changes the protocol. What a guess costs cites the owner's measured whole-operation times from mhfe commit 883373c. Owner's decision before the release: Part II is brought up to date for suite 3, changing only what no longer held (parameters, formulas, figures, implementation, measurements and vectors), and the released suite 2 text is kept in docs/archive/. After review: threat models T7 and T8, a table of what each recovery check confirms, the measured build revision, the limits of memory handling, the adopted packing separated from research alternatives, and the rare case in which the word count must be kept. The state-derived salts are related to NIST SP 800-132, reference [48], and to RFC 9106, without claiming conformance. Owner's decision after the threat-model review: threat models T9 to T15, related passwords under T5, and analyses of faults, many containers of many owners, leaks of intermediate values, observers on the same computer, determinism as a check on implementations, future attacks, losing access and repeated disclosures. After a further review: a second computer and an independent implementation are separated as checks for hardware faults and software errors, and the table of recovery checks distinguishes a known address from the weaker 32-bit fingerprint. Owner's decision after the deniability review: repeated disclosures and wallet checks, several containers of one phrase, evidence outside the model, the difference between removing evidence and deterring an adversary, and the Bayesian signalling game as a separate open question. After a further review: the example of a counted oracle call in a wallet check no longer implies that every deterministic signature uses HMAC-SHA-256, and open questions 7 and 8 name adaptive demands, outside evidence, the adversary's prior about the owner's wealth and the kinds of equilibria. Owner's decision after a review of likely questions: a damaged plate and heirs under Losing access, and quantum search and elliptic-curve keys under Attacks in the future. Consistency with the specification: salt uniqueness is stated for containers of independently generated sources, the rehearsal reads the finished backup, and recovery offers a manual choice of all five lengths. Editorial review: the main threat is the one analysed first rather than the only one that matters, the introduction no longer lists suite 2 differences, and the damaged-plate comparison is stated in terms of Argon2id work. Owner's decision to avoid duplication: the final-word section of Part I is a summary, with the purpose, the information revealed, the cheaper variants and the cost of password variants moved into the full analysis of Part II, and the start of Part II refers to the specification instead of repeating what recovery needs. The ordinary appearance of the container is called practical concealment, distinct from the plausible-deniability claim of Part I. After a further review: the expected number of checksum-valid candidates for one unreadable word other than the last counts the right word, about 1 + 2047/256, roughly nine, with the times recomputed. The formulas of Part II use the plain notation of the specification and Part I instead of GitHub LaTeX; every formula keeps its numbers and variables, with Ent for entropy, Ex for an expected value and Packed_ENT for the set of packed states, so that these do not clash with H, E and S_i. Table cells write concatenation as an escaped pipe, which a table needs even inside code, and the 24-word row of the packing table reads E_256 like the rows above it. The suite 2 vectors are named at vectors/archive/suite-2/. After the check of every cited source against its original: the three alternatives at the start of Part I are described through sufficient published bounds, with mixing between Lai-Massey rounds and Vaudenay's orthomorphism or almost orthomorphism; the Deniability section names how it is narrower than the definition of Canetti, Dwork, Naor and Ostrovsky; RFC 9106's procedure selects four lanes rather than beginning with them; BIP38 specifies rather than standardizes its format; the Hoang-Rogaway figure and appendix numbers are those of the 2018 ePrint revision, with Figure 7 for the Appendix E comparison. Renumbered the common bibliography by first citation in README.md followed by DESIGN-NOTES.md, preserving every citation-to-source association and all bibliographic content. Owner's decision to analyse suite 4: a section between Part I and Part II examines what the narrower state changes (salt diversity, shared salts, precomputation, known pairs, generic Feistel bounds, deniability, related containers of both suites, copying errors), states procedure costs rather than lower bounds, and adds open question 9; Part II points to suite 4 instead of saying that no such variant is planned. Theorems 1 and 2 are extended to suite 4 at every length, with fixed-point terms of 2^-ENT and HMAC key terms unchanged; the HMAC query count is renamed q; Conjecture 1 notes the h-bit hidden half of suite 4; the limits name the honest owner of each suite and the need for uniformly random entropy. Recorded the pending prior-art and citation corrections and bounded address-reference wording, then corrected the research proposals: container-digest notation, repair estimates and enumeration limits, independently trusted seals, settings-only checks, entropy-conditioning and nested-layer costs. Qualified mixed-KDF procedure costs; documented private password check words, bounded selection, recovery dependencies, independent emergency routes and intermediate state widths. Moved Research directions after implementation, vectors and limitations. These are subsequent document edits, not an extension of the original audit conclusions. 2026-10-05: User-authorized research clarification keeps MW a separate future program and publication; records independent BIP39 passphrases as additional protection; defines a candidate normalized length prefix included in the full password with separate secret cores; scopes seed check words and chosen-length readings; and qualifies MW capacity, false matches, salt reuse, rank retries, partial recovery, covert-channel mitigation, and unresolved deniability estimates. These documentation corrections do not change either suite algorithm or test vectors. 2026-10-05: Explicitly made derived-wallet check words voluntary and off by default in a future interface; creation and recovery require no check-word record, loss does not prevent recovery, and the ordinary wallet-reference confirmation remains available. 2026-10-05, AUD-007 documentation follow-up (outside the AUD-005 snapshot): the seed check is described as a statistical filter with its conditional entropy and decoy limits; the draft profile implemented in mhfe is defined to the byte with a public vector; the disclosure-simulation corollary is restricted to the synthetic experiment with a consistently programmed record oracle. The intermediate-width note mentioned above was removed again at the owner's request. 2026-10-05 AUD-007 follow-up: explicit base real-wallet record-oracle access and fresh-record scope for the simulation corollary; no normative suite algorithm change. Targeted corrections on 2026-10-06 consolidate the two reviewers' wording findings; suite algorithms, fenced formulas, vectors and bibliography are unchanged. Targeted optional-profile wording corrections on 2026-10-06 clarify repair decoding limits and candidate counts, password check-word disclosure, and profile status; algorithms and public vectors are unchanged. Owner-authorized clarification of suite identification and all five document-review remarks: six-position password repair and general validation, conditional multi-container reuse estimates, historical suite 3 implementation scope and current vector links, and limitations of both suites and the optional profiles. Prepared specification version 0.5.0 as unreleased, with consistent preamble, banner, changelog and citation metadata; the v0.4.0 DOI and release date remain archival. Algorithms and vector values are unchanged. +**What it is for.** The container would end with the same word as the original 24-word mnemonic. An
+owner who remembers the last word of each wallet could then tell which plate belongs to which wallet
+without decrypting anything. This would also be a quick check of a plate before any computation: a
+plate whose last word differs from the remembered one is not this wallet's container or was copied
+wrongly. It is an 11-bit check of the plate, not of the password or of the other 23 words, and it
+does not show that a recovery used the right password.
+
+**How it would work.** The permutation is applied again and again until the last word of the result
+matches the last word of the start, first during creation and then in the inverse direction during
+recovery:
+
+```text
+creation:                         recovery:
+  target = FW(X)                    target = FW(Y)
+  Y = Perm(X)                       X' = Perm^-1(Y)
+  while FW(Y) != target:            while FW(X') != target:
+      Y = Perm(Y)                       X' = Perm^-1(X')
+```
+
+`FW` is the 11-bit index of the last word: the last three entropy bits followed by the 8-bit BIP39
+checksum. The first application is mandatory, no counter is stored, and the walk fails if it returns
+to its start before finding another match. Suite 2 specified exactly this as the optional profile
+`MHFE-BIP39-256-EXPERIMENTAL-2-CYCLE-WALK-FINAL-WORD`; its full rules and analysis are in Part II.
+
+**What it risks.**
+
+- The last word reveals three bits of the source entropy directly and, through its 8-bit checksum,
+  about 11 bits of information about the source in total: the source is confined to a class of about
+  `2^245` values.
+- It does not confirm the password. A successful walk under a wrong password also returns a mnemonic
+  with the same last word.
+- The owner must remember that it was used. Standard recovery would silently produce a different
+  24-word wallet.
+- The number of steps depends on the password and the source, which creates a timing signal; Part II
+  quantifies it.
+
+**What it costs.** A match is expected after about 2,048 complete permutations, with a long tail and
+no practical upper bound. With the suite 3 parameters, at one to two minutes per permutation on the
+reference laptop, that is roughly one to two days at the median, one and a half to three days on
+average and up to about 13 days at the 99th percentile, for every recovery; a creation with its
+check walks the same way forward and back and takes about twice as long. Each password guess has a
+similarly large expected cost under this model, although individual walk lengths vary, so trying
+many variants of a half-remembered password is generally impractical.
+

+naturally. The first is a walk with a fast permutation and only one expensive Argon2id call to
+derive its key. The difficulty is the salt of that call. It must be computable from the original
+during creation and from the container during recovery, and the only thing the two share is the last
+word itself: 11 bits. There would therefore be only 2,048 possible salts in the world. An attacker
+could compute Argon2id for a password dictionary once per salt and then test every such container
+almost for free, which is exactly the shared dictionary that state-derived salts exist to prevent.

+recovery the backward walk has no way to recognise where the expensive part ended. The third is to
+find a matching container cheaply with light parameters and then look for a way to reach it with the

+permutations instead of 2,048 but requires a new permutation and its own analysis.

-Suite 4 keeps the source's length: its state is the source entropy, `ENT` = 128, 160, 192 or 224

-section examines what the narrower halves change compared with suite 3. It is an analysis in the
-same spirit as Part I, not a proof. The deniability theorems of Part I extend to suite 4, as stated
-in [the suite 4 extension](#suite-4-the-same-analysis-at-every-length); the conjectures on attack
-cost are not asserted for it.
-
-**Salt diversity.** For fixed settings and round index a salt is a function of one `h`-bit half, so
-it takes at most `2^h` values, `2^64` for a 12-word source; this is an upper bound on its diversity,
-not a guarantee of `h` bits of randomness. RFC 9106 permits a 64-bit salt length under space
-constraints [4]. This provides context, not a security justification for suite 4: its salts remain
-128 bits long but are derived from an `h`-bit state half, and their distribution, correlations and
-reuse require construction-specific analysis.
-

-round comes from the container's left half `L_12`, which anyone holding the container can read. For
-containers with the same `ENT` and settings whose halves are independent and uniformly random, the
-expected number of pairs with equal left halves among `N` containers is `N(N - 1) / 2^(h+1)`: about
-one half for `N = 2^32` containers of 12 words, with a probability of about 39 % that at least one
-such pair exists, and correspondingly fewer for longer sources. An ideal random permutation maps any
-fixed source to a uniform container, but the actual construction's bijectivity alone does not
-establish this distribution: a fixed permutation maps uniform source entropy to uniform container

-guess on both containers of such a pair by full recovery takes 23 Argon2id calls instead of 24, and
-a group of `g` containers with the same left half saves `g - 1` calls for that round. Coincidences
-of the salts of other rounds depend on states that change with every password; they cannot be found
-in advance, but they can be detected during a search, and with a known source the salt of the first
-round is known as well. Whether such coincidences allow a larger saving across many containers has
-not been shown either way.

-#### Losing access
-
-Losing access is a risk of its own, independent of any attacker. Recovery needs the container, the
-password, any non-default settings, the original word count in the rare case of an ambiguous length,
-and software that implements the suite, possibly decades later. The BIP39 checksum detects most
-copying errors but corrects none. The optional
-[MHFE-REPAIR-1 card](../README.md#optional-repair-words-mhfe-repair-1) can repair unreadable or
-wrong words within the code's bound; it is not needed for an intact container and does not replace a
-second complete copy. The rehearsal check of the specification, a password recalled from time to
-time, a copy of the container in a second place and an offline copy of a compatible release reduce
-these risks.
-
-**A recovery plan.** Record the suite, settings, source length, password format, compatible offline
-software, and how to retrieve a trusted wallet reference and any separate BIP39 passphrase. Check
-scenarios in which a location is destroyed, the main container copy is lost, the password is
-forgotten, the owner cannot help an heir, or the original computer is unavailable. Instructions,
-password backups, references and software must be accessible without first opening this wallet or
-using the secret whose loss they are meant to remedy. Rehearse the plan from the finished backup;
-instructions do not replace missing secrets.
-
-**A damaged plate.** If one word of a container cannot be read and its position is known, about
-`1 + 2047 / 256`, roughly nine, of the 2,048 possible words give a valid BIP39 checksum, counting
-the right one, and exactly eight if it is the last word. Each candidate needs a full recovery: about
-9 to 18 minutes in total at the default settings on the reference laptop, and about 6 to 13 days at
-PIM 1023. Two unreadable words give about 16,400 candidates, roughly 11 to 23 days of continuous
-computation at the default settings. A short source's verifier will normally reject every wrong
-candidate, subject to the false-match and ambiguity probabilities given in the specification; for a
-24-word source each recovered phrase has to be compared with a known address or other trusted wallet
-data. For an ordinary phrase with the same damage, the candidates need no Argon2id work and can be
-checked against the wallet directly. A second copy of the container is therefore worth more with
-MHFE than without it, and it should be an exact copy of the same verified container, not a second
-encryption of the phrase, for the reasons given under [Deniability](#deniability).
-
-**Heirs.** A plate that holds a container looks like an ordinary phrase. An heir who does not know
-that it is a container would enter it in a wallet, find an empty wallet or a decoy, and might
-conclude that nothing is there. An heir has to learn separately that the plate is an MHFE container,
-which suite and settings it uses, the password, and where to find compatible software. Marking the
-plate as an MHFE container helps the heir. It does not weaken the deniability proofs, which already
-assume that the adversary knows that MHFE is used, but it reveals that use, can raise an adversary's
-suspicion and removes the option of presenting the container as an ordinary phrase. How these facts
-are passed on involves the same trade-off.
-
-**An independent emergency route.** A separate threshold backup of the original entropy, retaining
-its source length and wordlist, or an encrypted source backup with an independently random,
-threshold-shared key could survive loss of all usable MHFE-password knowledge and all container
-copies. A sufficient coalition obtains the source without those artifacts; individual holders below
-the threshold do not. Any separate BIP39 passphrase still needs a recovery arrangement. This adds
-custody and software dependencies, and protection is limited by the weakest complete recovery route.
-A forgotten password and a lost main plate can also be remedied by a secure full-password backup and
-another exact container copy through the ordinary route. An independent route is needed when every
-means of recovering the ordinary route's required material has been lost. The current deniability
-experiments do not cover these additional recovery artifacts.

+match, fall back to an unverified 24-word interpretation when none matches, and report every
+matching short length when detection is ambiguous. Explicit source length remains available as an
+override; detailed vector-trace recovery requires it because the trace result is profile-specific.
+
+Version 0.3.1 of the library, CLI, direct WASM API, and Worker client also implements the optional
+final-word-preserving profile. It restricts creation to 24-word sources, reports progress after each
+complete permutation, supports cancellation between permutations, and requires an explicit profile
+choice for recovery. The standard suite-2 APIs and published suite-2 vectors remain unchanged.
+
+The operational Rust API and the explicitly test-only vector API use separate result types. The
+operational result does not expose source entropy, packed plaintext, Argon2 outputs, round masks, or
+round traces. Reachable Rust-owned password, mnemonic, entropy, round-material, result, and Argon2
+work buffers are zeroized on their relevant drop or reuse paths. This is a memory-hygiene measure
+rather than a guarantee that compilers, allocators, browser strings, operating systems, or earlier
+reallocations leave no residual copies. Allocation failure is returned as a typed error when the
+initial Argon2 work-area reservation fails. The implementation also rejects an unchanged encrypted
+state rather than returning a fixed point as a usable backup.
+
+The CLI's direct string-input path intentionally accepts ASCII test passwords only. ASCII is
+unchanged by Unicode 18 NFKD, while the available Rust normalization tables currently implement
+Unicode 17. The library and browser API also accept UTF-8 bytes already normalized by a conforming
+Unicode 18 NPSS-NFKD implementation, but do not claim to verify that precondition. Rejecting
+non-ASCII text on the self-normalizing path avoids silently producing vectors that fail the
+specification's pinned NPSS-NFKD-Unicode-18.0.0 rule.
+
+The implementation is not finalized or independently reviewed by a cryptography specialist, and it
+is not independent evidence for its own vectors. A separately written Python scratch verifier
+derived only from this specification has reproduced all nine published vectors and intermediate
+values in both directions. That is a limited interoperability cross-check, not a maintained second
+implementation or a security review. A toy reduced-width model must not be used as evidence of
+production security.

 ### Known Limitations
 
-This section records the present boundaries of both experimental suites and the optional profiles.
-It is not a roadmap and does not commit the author to further research or implementation work.
-
-- The selected Argon2id and Feistel parameters are supported by limited measurements on the author's
-  laptop.
-- Suite 3's short-source recovery verifiers intentionally provide an offline password-checking
-  signal, while its ordinary 24-word source mode has no internal wrong-password test and automatic
-  source-length detection remains probabilistic. Its reference APIs implement automatic detection
-  and retain explicit source length as an override.
-- Suite 4 has no built-in verifier at any supported length. Its narrower states limit salt
-  diversity, reveal the source's word count and require separate analysis of password filters and
-  shared work; see [the narrower-state analysis](#suite-4-what-the-narrower-state-changes).
-- The optional source check for new 24-word wallets is a 16-bit statistical filter, not confirmation
-  of wallet identity. It conditions the source distribution, and the deniability theorems for
-  uniformly generated sources do not automatically apply. With a nonempty passphrase it checks the
-  recovered mnemonic and passphrase together; with the empty passphrase it filters MHFE password
-  guesses alone.
-- Repair words and the password check word add redundancy, not authentication. They repair only
-  within their stated bounds, and disclosure of that redundancy reveals information about the
-  container or password respectively. Passing either check does not establish the intended wallet.
